source: Chase & Simon (1973) Perception in Chess. Cognitive Psychology 4
finding: Founding experiment. Three players (master M, Class A, beginner B) rebuilt 20 game positions (10 middle game with 24-26 pieces, 10 end game with 12-15 pieces) after a 5 s view, with repeated trials. Recall of real positions rose steeply with skill.
numbers: First trial, middle game: M about 16 pieces correct, A about 8, B about 4. End game: M about 8, A about 7, B about 4. M needed 3-4 trials to be perfect, A one or two more, B up to 14.
limits: Only N=3 players, 5 positions per cell. Positions included non-quiet ones and games of weaker players, which depressed the master's score.
agent_relevance: The expert edge is fast, domain-matched encoding, not general memory. An agent gains most from stored domain patterns, and the gain shows on first exposure.

source: Chase & Simon (1973) Perception in Chess. Cognitive Psychology 4 (replication of de Groot on quiet puzzle positions)
finding: Using nine quiet positions from a puzzle book (Reinfeld 1945), results matched de Groot's published figures. The lower scores on the first set came from messy positions with exchanges under way.
numbers: Single 5 s trial: B, A, M averaged 33, 49, 81 percent correct on quiet positions versus 18, 34, 62 percent on the first set. de Groot's masters placed about 23-24 of 25 pieces after 5 s or less; M here averaged 16 on the harder set.
limits: Tiny N. Procedure differed from de Groot: he told players who was on move and they viewed from that side.
agent_relevance: The effect depends on stimulus typicality. An agent test must use typical, well-formed cases or it will understate expertise.

source: Chase & Simon (1973) Perception in Chess. Cognitive Psychology 4 (random positions)
finding: With the same pieces shuffled randomly there was no link between skill and recall. First-trial recall on random positions was worse than the beginner's score on real positions. The master also did no better on positions he recognised within 1 s (83 vs 79 percent).
numbers: Random positions: no relation to playing strength in the three subjects; all below the beginner's real-position level. Recognised vs unrecognised: 83 vs 79 percent (M, 9 new positions, 4 recognised).
limits: Later work (Gobet & Simon 1996) shows a small skill effect does exist with random positions; N=3 had no power to see it.
agent_relevance: Experts are not better at raw storage. Structure that matches stored patterns is what is cheap to hold. A check of whether input resembles known patterns predicts when recall will work.

source: Chase & Simon (1973) Perception in Chess. Cognitive Psychology 4 (pause-based chunk definition)
finding: Two tasks gave the chunk operationalisation. In the perception task (copy a board in view) one glance equals one chunk. In the memory task a gap of 2 s or more between placed pieces marks a chunk boundary. Interpiece interval distributions in the two tasks were similar.
numbers: Within-glance intervals seldom above 2 s. Between-glance means: M 2.8 s, A 3.2 s, B 3.5 s (p<.05). Dansereau estimate cited: about 2 s to start a chunk, about 300 ms per element. Between-subject correlations of relation probabilities .89 to .95.
limits: Pause-based segmentation is indirect. Picking pieces off the side of the board takes at least 1 s, an acknowledged artefact. Oral and paper versions were said to give the same result but were not reported.
agent_relevance: Gives a measurable proxy for chunk size from output timing. The agent analogue is to chunk by structure in its own trace, not by length.

source: Chase & Simon (1973) Perception in Chess. Cognitive Psychology 4 (what a chunk is)
finding: Pieces placed together within a chunk tend to share several chess relations: attack, defence, adjacency, same colour, same type. Pawn chains were the clearest case. Pairs across chunk boundaries had few relations, near chance.
numbers: Five relations over 16 combinations per pair. Observed vs a priori probabilities differ strongly (z up to about 21 for some multi-relation pairs). Same pattern at all three skill levels (r .92-.95).
limits: The relation list is the authors' own choice. Chunks may be coded by other features such as piece-square location.
agent_relevance: Chunks are relational units, not raw clusters. A scaffold that groups evidence by explicit relations such as supports, attacks, depends-on may mirror this.

source: de Groot (1946/1965) Thought and Choice in Chess, as reported by Chase & Simon 1973 and Charness et al. 2001
finding: de Groot found no gross difference in search between masters and weaker players: similar number of moves considered, depth and heuristics, masters not searching more. The difference was in which moves came to mind and in recall of briefly shown positions. He concluded perception and memory, not look-ahead, separate experts. Read only through secondary descriptions, not the book itself.
numbers: Recall after 2-15 s view: best players about 93 percent correct on positions of about 25 pieces (Charness 2001 summary); 23-24 of 25 pieces (Chase & Simon 1973 summary).
limits: Book not opened; numbers are second-hand. The original sample was small and the search finding was later partly revised (see the 2011 replication).
agent_relevance: Strong case that better thinking is mostly better retrieval of the right candidate, not deeper search. Favours retrieval of good first candidates plus a small search budget.

source: Simon & Chase (1973) Skill in Chess. American Scientist 61
finding: Popular statement of the chunking theory: short-term memory holds about seven chunks (labels pointing to long-term memory); a master needs a large repertoire of familiar patterns; a new chunk takes about 5 s to learn; a perception program links patterns to move generation. Only fragments of a column-scrambled scan were read.
numbers: STM about 7 chunks. About 5 s per new chunk (8 s in later EPAM numbers). The 50,000-chunk figure was traced through Gobet & Simon 1996 to Simon & Gilmartin 1973.
limits: Text scan was scrambled, so only fragments were read. The 50,000 figure is an order-of-magnitude estimate, not measured.
agent_relevance: Frames skill as large pattern store plus fast recognition plus selective search, which matches a retrieval library plus a small search budget.

source: Gobet & Simon (1996) Templates in chess memory. Cognitive Psychology 31 (review of Chase-Simon and its problems)
finding: States the chunking model: experts hold about 50,000 chunks, STM about seven. Lists three challenges: interference studies, level-of-processing studies, and blindfold or multi-board play. Charness (1976) found only a 6-8 percent loss after a 30 s delay. Frey & Adesman (1976) found small loss after counting backward. Bradley et al. (1987): a verbal task had minimal effect but visuospatial or central-executive load cut recall by more than two thirds.
numbers: Charness: 6-8 percent drop versus a large drop for trigrams. Frey & Adesman: about 10 pieces per position for two boards at 8 s each; chunking fits this with 5-10 s per chunk. Bradley: more than 2/3 decline under visuospatial interference.
limits: Several level-of-processing results (Goldin 1978; Frey & Adesman 1976) are confounded with extra viewing time.
agent_relevance: Competing explanations to a pure STM chunk story exist. Capacity limits are soft; the useful constraint is load on the right channel, not a fixed count.

source: Gobet & Simon (1996) Templates in chess memory. Cognitive Psychology 31 Experiment 1 (several boards)
finding: 13 players (3 Masters mean Elo 2453, 4 Experts 2180, 6 Class A 1883) saw up to five positions for 5 s each. Recall percentage fell with more boards, but masters recalled far more than seven chunks allow. Random-position recall was not significantly related to skill at this N.
numbers: Skill F(2,10)=22.47, p<.001; boards F(4,40)=9.11. Random single position: Masters 21 percent, Experts 16, Class A 12 (F(2,10)=3.46, ns). Masters placed up to 60 pieces, Experts about 40, Class A under 20. Chunks (pieces placed within 2 s): 2.3 with one board to 9.9 with five for Experts and Masters; individuals up to 13-15 chunks. Largest chunk: Masters 19.7 pieces for one board vs 12.4 for several.
limits: Small N. One Grandmaster lost a trial to a lapse (Masters at five boards 50 percent after discarding). Chunk count uses a conservative 2 s rule.
agent_relevance: Direct evidence that expert recall exceeds fixed-size STM. Retrieval structures matter more than a fixed chunk count, so offer indexed slots rather than a flat list.

source: Gobet & Simon (1996) Templates in chess memory. Cognitive Psychology 31 Experiment 2 (delay between boards)
finding: Five players (one GM, one IM, others) saw two or four boards with 1, 2, 5 or 10 s gaps. More time between boards helped, much more for Masters than Experts. Single-board recall matched Experiment 1.
numbers: One game position: Masters 92.3 percent, Experts 64.5. One random position: Masters 21.1, Experts 17.7. Gain from 1 s to 10 s gap: Masters 71 percent (2 boards), 63 percent (4 boards); Experts 40 and 33 percent. At 10 s and four boards (100 pieces): Masters 82.9 pieces, Experts 44.9.
limits: N=5. Masters' 5 s result lowered by one GM missing a board. Latency order was counterbalanced with no effect.
agent_relevance: Experts use spare time to link new input to existing structure. More budget helps a pattern-rich agent more than a pattern-poor one.

source: Gobet & Simon (1996) Templates in chess memory. Cognitive Psychology 31 Experiment 3 (Chessmaster, many boards)
finding: One Chessmaster practised a multi-board task over about 150 sessions across 37 weeks. He built a retrieval structure: a cue list of 13 world champions, each linked to a board by an association. Performance rose to nine boards at over 70 percent accuracy.
numbers: Over 160 pieces correct in four sessions: 163 (9 boards), 160 (10 boards), 167 (9), 178 (9). Two-board warm-up from 40 pieces (80 percent) to 47 (94 percent). Multi-board: 44 pieces after block 1, 79 at block 4, 152 at block 18, plateau near 123.
limits: N=1 and a trained mnemonist with a self-made cue list. Not a test of natural expertise.
agent_relevance: Strong model of an explicit retrieval structure: slots that bind items to stable cues. Fits a schema with named state slots and bounded notes per slot.

source: Gobet & Simon (1996) Templates in chess memory. Cognitive Psychology 31 (template theory)
finding: Template theory extends chunking. Large frequent chunks become templates: a fixed core of about a dozen pieces plus slots for pieces, squares, opening, plan and move, with links to other templates. Filling a slot is fast (under 1 s). A new chunk costs about 8 s. A random position rarely evokes templates, so masters' edge there shrinks but does not vanish.
numbers: Core about 12 pieces. Slot fill under 1 s (250 ms in CHREST). New retrieval path about 8 s. 50,000 or more chunks.
limits: Templates are inferred from fits, not observed. Single-template and multi-template variants were both considered.
agent_relevance: A template with slots is close to an agent schema: fixed core plus variable slots filled at read time. Supports typed scratch slots over free notes.

source: Gobet & Simon (1996) Recall of random and distorted chess positions. Memory & Cognition 24 (mirror-image test)
finding: CHREST predicted that reflecting a game position around the vertical axis (or both axes) would hurt recall because chunks hold specific squares, with horizontal reflection hurting less. Human players (about 25, three skill levels) confirmed it. Chunks are tied to exact locations, so concept-only knowledge does not explain recall.
numbers: Normal and horizontal: Masters 77.3, Experts 49.7, Class A 34.5 percent; vertical and central: 62.9, 38.6, 27.5 percent. Skill F(2,22)=24.52, modification F(3,66)=20.85 (both p<.001). Drop 10.3 percent in humans vs 11.4 percent in simulation. No condition fell to random-position level.
limits: Colour is also encoded, so horizontal flips are not neutral. Chunk-size differences were not significant.
agent_relevance: Pattern memory is brittle to small layout changes inside the expert's own domain. Test agent retrieval under paraphrase and reordering.

source: Gobet & Simon (1996) Recall of random and distorted chess positions. Memory & Cognition 24 (CHREST simulation)
finding: CHREST learns a discrimination net of chunks by sorting pieces seen in 20 random fixations (about 5 s for humans). Recall rises as a log function of net size and predicts a small advantage even on random positions.
numbers: Nets grew to 70,000 nodes. Recall = a + b log(nodes) explained over 98 percent of variance in all four position types. Random-position recall rose slightly, to 23.4 percent. Supports 50,000 chunks for masters.
limits: The 50,000 figure rests on model parameters. Colour was assumed encoded in chunks.
agent_relevance: A log law in chunk count means diminishing returns from library size, useful for sizing a pattern library.

source: Gobet & Waters (2003) The role of constraints in expert memory. JEP:LMC 29 (fully random positions)
finding: Vicente & Wang (1998) argued the skill effect on random chess positions comes from leftover environmental constraints and should vanish with truly random placement. Template theory predicted a small effect remains. 36 players of widely varied skill recalled five position types for 5 s. A skill effect remained with fully random pieces and squares.
numbers: Truly random positions: r=.34 (p<.025, one-tailed); slope 0.052 per rating point (SE 0.016), about 5.2 percent more recall per 100 rating points, versus the model's 0.061 (6.1 percent, roughly 1.5 pieces). Model slopes: game .331, 1/3 .216, 2/3 .077, random .071, 3/3 .061. R2 28 percent for 3/3 with age and visual memory.
limits: Effects are small; age and visual memory also entered the regression. The constraint view is not fully ruled out for the less random conditions.
agent_relevance: A model made a new prediction and data confirmed it. Supports building agents from small learned units, not only high-level descriptions.

source: Gobet & Waters (2003) The role of constraints in expert memory. JEP:LMC 29 (descriptive numbers)
finding: Game-position recall rises strongly with skill; random-position recall only slightly. Skill correlates far more with game than random recall.
numbers: Game: GMs 83.7 percent (SD 14.4), masters/experts 61.3, Class A/B 55.1, Class C/D 40.1. Random: 18.3, 17.0, 14.1, 12.3. Fully random: 14.8, 16.3, 13.7, 12.0. r=.68 for game vs r=.36 for random.
limits: Rating and age were correlated (r=.38). Seven guessers did not differ from others.
agent_relevance: Gives the size of the random-position floor, which can serve as a null baseline in LLM tests.

source: Gobet & Simon (2000) Five seconds or sixty? Presentation time in expert memory. Cognitive Science 24
finding: 21 players (Elo 1770-2595) saw game and random positions for 1 to 60 s. CHREST, with fixed EPAM time parameters, predicted the curves. Masters reach a ceiling after about 3 s on game positions; weaker players keep improving over 60 s. The skill effect on random positions is clearer at long exposures.
numbers: Masters at 1 s equal Experts at 10 s on game positions. Parameter learned in 1 s is 2x larger for Masters than Class A and the rate c triples. Masters' chunk count 4.5 at 10 s then 2.9 at 60 s (bigger chunks). CHREST: 50 ms to encode a chunk to STM, 250 ms into a template slot, about 8 s to learn a chunk.
limits: Parameters come from earlier EPAM fits, but mapping to human timing is approximate. Long-term working memory theory predicts too strong random performance.
agent_relevance: Time budget matters differently by skill: an expert agent saturates fast, a novice agent keeps gaining. Stop early on strong pattern hits; continue on unfamiliar items.

source: Gobet & Clarkson (2004) Chunks in expert memory: evidence for the magical number four or is it two? Memory 12
finding: Tests chunking vs template theory on how many chunks fit in short-term memory and how big they are, using copy and recall with a physical board and a computer screen. Fewer than three chunks were placed in most conditions. Masters on screen placed very large chunks (up to 15 pieces).
numbers: Fewer than three chunks in recall for most skill levels and conditions; random positions 1.3 to 2.1 chunks; largest Master chunks up to 15 pieces on screen. Authors say Cowan's four may be an overestimate.
limits: Chunk count depends on the 2 s pause rule and display medium. Chase & Simon used only three players.
agent_relevance: Supports small working capacity with big structured units. Limit active slots; make each slot rich.

source: Richman, Staszewski & Simon (1995) Simulation of expert memory using EPAM IV. Psychological Review 102
finding: EPAM IV adds retrieval structures and associative search to the chunking net. It reproduces a digit-span expert (DD) who reached 104 digits after about 865 practice sessions over more than three years, using a tree-like retrieval structure with leaves holding 3-4 digit chunks and running-time codes.
numbers: About 865 sessions to 104 digits at about one digit per second. Four-level retrieval structure (digits, chunks, supergroups, supergroup clusters) per Gobet et al. 2015.
limits: Single-subject data; symbolic hand-tuned model.
agent_relevance: Capacity grew through a learned retrieval structure plus semantic chunk codes, not a larger STM. Useful pattern for how the scaffold organises memory.

source: Gobet, Lane & Lloyd-Kelly (2015) Chunks, schemata, and retrieval structures: past and current computational models. Frontiers in Psychology 6:1785
finding: Compares verbal theories with computer models. When Ericsson & Kintsch's long-term working memory theory was implemented (Gobet 2000), recall ranged from 10 to 100 percent on both game and random positions depending on parameters, so the verbal theory was nearly unfalsifiable. CHREST's random-position prediction was confirmed. Saariluoma (1989), pieces dictated at 2 s each: over 80 percent for game and at most 60 percent for random positions.
numbers: LTWM implementation: 10-100 percent recall over parameters. Saariluoma: over 80 vs no more than 60. CHREST learns hundreds of thousands of chunks in minutes. Chunk definition: a meaningful unit built from smaller pieces of the same kind.
limits: Opinion piece by the CHREST group, favouring chunk-network models. The word chunk has many meanings (ACT-R declarative unit, Soar procedural unit).
agent_relevance: Warns that vague schema ideas cannot be tested. Our schema should state slot sizes, timings and counts so it can be falsified.

source: Sala & Gobet (2017) Experts' memory superiority for domain-specific random material generalizes across fields of expertise: a meta-analysis. Memory & Cognition 45
finding: Across 28 effects, expertise correlates with recall of random domain material, as small chunks predict. The effect holds in games, music and programming; it is not significant in sports and other domains. Also cites an earlier 13-study chess meta-analysis (Gobet & Simon 1996b).
numbers: Overall r=.41, 95 percent CI [.29, .51], k=28, I2=63 percent. Games r=.42 (k=11), music r=.69 (k=5), programming r=.36 (k=6), sports r=.30 (k=3, ns), other r=.24 (k=3, ns). Domain moderator Q(4)=8.69, p=.069. Sensitivity r=.39 (k=26). Fail-safe N 745.
limits: Moderate heterogeneity. Exposure time was not a significant moderator. Only chess uses a continuous Elo measure.
agent_relevance: Gives a replicated size for the random-material effect, about r .4. Use as the human baseline when checking whether an LLM shows a skill gain on shuffled input.

source: Charness, Reingold, Pomplun & Stampe (2001) The perceptual aspect of skilled performance in chess: evidence from eye movements. Memory & Cognition 29
finding: 24 players (12 experts rated 2100-2350, 12 intermediates) chose the best move in five positions with eye tracking. Experts used half as many fixations, made longer jumps, and looked more at empty squares and relevant pieces. No difference in fixation duration.
numbers: Experts 11.7 s vs 23.4 s; 4.75 vs 3.33 of 5 correct; fixations per trial 44.3 vs 83.6; fixation duration 253 vs 244 ms (ns); fixations on empty squares .52 vs .41; on salient pieces .80 vs .64 (t(22), p<.05 or better).
limits: Five mate-in-few positions only. Earlier work (de Groot & Gobet 1996) found shorter fixations for experts; this study did not.
agent_relevance: Experts attend by relevance using wide-view chunks. In an agent: a first pass over the whole input that marks salient items before detailed reading.

source: Bilalic, McLeod & Gobet (2007) Does chess need intelligence? A study with young chess players. Intelligence 35
finding: 57 young players: practice had the most influence on rating; IQ explained some variance after practice in the full sample. In the elite subsample (n=23) IQ was not significant and tended to correlate negatively with rating, because IQ and practice correlated negatively there.
numbers: N=57 (WISC III, practice, experience); elite n=23.
limits: Children, cross-sectional, selection effects in the elite group.
agent_relevance: Supports expertise as built by domain practice. An agent should accumulate domain patterns, not rely on general ability alone.

source: Connors, Burns & Campitelli (2011) Expertise in complex decision making: the role of search in chess 70 years after de Groot. Cognitive Science 35
finding: Replication of de Groot's think-aloud study: 6 Grandmasters, 5 International Masters, 6 Experts, 5 Class A players, two positions each. GMs and IMs search faster than weaker players and all search much faster than in earlier studies, but de Groot's overall conclusion stands and fits pattern-recognition models. Abstract only, via OpenAlex.
numbers: N=22 players, two positions each; no figures read.
limits: Abstract only. Speed differences revise the no-difference claim for speed, not for depth.
agent_relevance: A modern check that retrieval beats search. Keep search shallow with strong first candidates.

source: Ruoss et al. (2024) Amortized planning with large-scale transformers: a case study on chess. arXiv 2402.04494
finding: Transformers trained on 10M Lichess games annotated by Stockfish 16 (about 15 billion data points) play without search. Bigger models are better and generalise to boards not seen in training. This is the scaling analogue of the expert's chunk store: more learned patterns, more skill, no deliberate search.
numbers: 9M: tournament Elo 2025, puzzle accuracy 88.9 percent. 136M: 2259, 94.5. 270M: 2299, 95.4, blitz Elo 2895 vs humans. GPT-3.5-turbo-instruct: puzzle 66.5, Elo 1755 vs bots. Leela policy net only 2292, puzzles 88.6. Stockfish 16 (50 ms) 2711.
limits: Engine labels, not human games. Search-free play shows odd endgame behaviour (does not take the fastest mate). Not a test of recall or chunking.
agent_relevance: A pattern store can replace search at expert level on a narrow task. Whether a prompted general LLM uses patterns the same way is open.

source: Karvonen (2024) Emergent world models and latent variable estimation in chess-playing language models. arXiv 2403.15498
finding: GPTs trained only on chess game text keep an internal board that linear probes can read. They also estimate player skill. Adding the skill direction raises win rate up to 2.6 times. Board-state interventions raise legal-move rate.
numbers: 16-layer model: legal move rate 99.8 percent, win rate 64 percent vs Stockfish level 0 (about 1300 Elo); 8-layer 46 percent. Probes: board square accuracy 99.6 (16-layer) vs 74.7 for a randomised model; Elo classification (below 1550 vs above 2050) 90.5 vs 69.3. Intervention: up to 92 percent legal moves vs about 41 without.
limits: Small custom models, not general LLMs. Skill probe is a binary split in a narrow Elo range.
agent_relevance: Models hold structured board state, an LLM analogue of chunk-level encoding. The scaffold should still check with output, not trust it.

source: McGrath et al. (2022) Acquisition of chess knowledge in AlphaZero. PNAS / arXiv 2111.09259
finding: Probing found human chess concepts represented in the AlphaZero network, with analysis of when they appear in training and where. Abstract page only.
numbers: No numbers read.
limits: Abstract only. Not a language model; a self-play RL network.
agent_relevance: Concepts resembling human chunks emerge during training, so agent patterns could be checked by probing.

source: Pleiss, Schiffer & von Weizsaecker (2026) Trapped in the past? Disentangling fluid and crystallized intelligence of LLMs using chess. arXiv 2601.16823
finding: Tests whether LLM skill is recall (familiar positions) or reasoning (novel positions). 500 positions per condition: within-distribution (Lichess masters database), near-distribution (10 random moves from start), out-of-distribution (ten pieces per side placed at random). Performance collapses toward random as positions get less familiar. Reasoning effort helps familiar positions most.
numbers: Average centipawn loss (illegal=1000): GPT-3.5 807.97, GPT-4o 540.38, GPT-5 463.5. Near-distribution CPL 4.75x within; out-of-distribution 7.79x. Legal move rate 25.3, 58.4, 66.2 percent. GPT-5 moderate reasoning: within 11.72 CPL vs out-of-distribution 298.81. Reasoning tokens 3,426 / 11,800 / 16,953.
limits: Only GPT models, training data unknown, out-of-distribution positions are tactical and unnatural. Preprint with inconsistencies (GPT-4 vs GPT-4o, an undefined 370.59 percent figure). Read through a page summary, not the full PDF.
agent_relevance: Closest LLM analogue of the random-position control: the expert advantage shrinks off the pattern store. Expect scaffold help to be largest on familiar structure and use outside checks off distribution.

source: Hu et al. (2024) HiAgent: hierarchical working memory management for solving long-horizon agent tasks with LLM. arXiv 2408.09559 (ACL 2025)
finding: Uses subgoals as memory chunks: keep the full action-observation history only for the current subgoal, replace finished subgoals by a summary, retrieve old detail on demand. Motivated by Miller-style chunking.
numbers: Success rate 42 vs 21 percent averaged over five long-horizon tasks (twofold); average steps reduced by 3.8; GPT-4 backbone. Removing trajectory retrieval cut success by 10 percent.
limits: Planning tasks, not memory recall tests. Chunk here means a subgoal summary, a loose use of the term.
agent_relevance: Direct use of chunking in an LLM agent, close to a schema that closes a subgoal into a summary slot with recall on demand.
